title: Design a Distributed Key-Value Store
summary: End-to-end walkthrough of a Dynamo-style store: consistent hashing with vnodes, N/R/W quorums, hinted handoff, conflict resolution, Merkle-tree repair and an LSM engine.
body:
## Practice first

Design a distributed key-value store that application teams use as a shared database: `put(key, value)`, `get(key)`, `delete(key)`, spread across many machines in several availability zones, staying writable when machines fail. Think of the shape of Amazon's Dynamo, Apache Cassandra or Riak rather than a single-node cache.

Spend about 10 minutes first: how do keys map to machines, how many copies exist, what does a read return when copies disagree, and how does a node store data on disk? Then compare.

## Functional requirements

Core (users should be able to):

1. **Put** a value (up to 1 MB, typically ~1 KB) under a key, overwriting any previous value.
2. **Get** the current value for a key, or "not found".
3. **Delete** a key.

Clients may also choose a **consistency level per request** (for example, read from one replica for speed, or from a quorum for freshness).

Out of scope: range scans and secondary indexes, multi-key transactions, a query language, and cross-region replication (we design one region with three zones and mention multi-region at the end).

## Non-functional requirements

- **Scale:** 10 billion keys, about 10 TB of logical data, 1 million operations per second (70% reads), growing 2× per year without downtime.
- **Latency:** p99 under 10 ms for single-key gets and puts within the region.
- **Availability over consistency for writes:** writes must succeed even when a replica or a whole zone is down ("always writable", like a shopping cart). Reads are eventually consistent by default; quorum reads give read-your-writes when no failures are in progress. This is a deliberate AP choice; we will say exactly where it leaks.
- **Durability:** an acknowledged write survives the loss of any single machine and any single zone.
- **Elasticity:** adding or removing nodes moves only a proportional share of data.

## Back-of-the-envelope

- **Storage:** 10 TB × 3 replicas = 30 TB. With ~2 TB of usable SSD per node and 50% headroom for compaction and growth, we need about **30 nodes**, 10 per zone. That decides that we need automatic partitioning and rebalancing, not manual sharding.
- **Throughput per node:** 1M ops/s × (replication fan-out: 3 for writes, 2 for quorum reads) ≈ 2.3M replica-ops/s ÷ 30 nodes ≈ **77k ops/s per node**. That is achievable with an append-only storage engine on SSDs but not with random in-place B-tree writes plus fsync per write, which drives the **LSM-tree** choice.
- **Rebalancing:** adding one node to 30 should move about 1/31 of the data (~1 TB of replicas), not most of it, which rules out `hash(key) mod N`.

## Core entities

- **Key / value / version:** the stored record, with version metadata (a timestamp or a vector clock) and a tombstone flag for deletes.
- **Node:** a storage server with an ID, zone and a set of virtual nodes (tokens) on the ring.
- **Partition (token range):** a slice of the hash ring; each has a preference list of N replica nodes.
- **Membership view:** which nodes exist and which are believed up, spread by gossip.

## API

Clients use a thin library (or any node acting as coordinator) over a binary RPC; HTTP is shown for readability.

```http
PUT /v1/kv/{key}?w=quorum
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
If-Match: <context>          (optional causal context from a previous get)
<bytes>
204 No Content
ETag: <new context>

GET /v1/kv/{key}?r=quorum
200 OK
ETag: <context>
<bytes>
300 Multiple Choices        (siblings, if the store keeps concurrent versions)

DELETE /v1/kv/{key}?w=quorum
204 No Content
```

`r` and `w` accept `one`, `quorum` or `all`. The opaque context carries the version the client last saw so the server can tell an update from a concurrent write. Authentication is per-tenant with mTLS; keys are namespaced by tenant.

## High-level design

**Partitioning.** Hash every key with a uniform hash (for example, Murmur3 or MD5 used only for distribution) onto a ring of 2^64 positions. Each physical node owns many **virtual nodes** (say 256 tokens), so load evens out and a failed node's ranges are spread over many peers.

**Replication.** A key's **preference list** is the first N = 3 distinct physical nodes walking clockwise from its hash, chosen so the three replicas sit in three different zones.

**Requests.** Any node can be a **coordinator**: the client library hashes the key and sends the request straight to one of its replicas (token-aware routing), which forwards to the others.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CL["Client library (token-aware)"] --> CO["Coordinator node"]
    CO --> R1["Replica A, zone 1"]
    CO --> R2["Replica B, zone 2"]
    CO --> R3["Replica C, zone 3"]
    R1 --> S1[("LSM storage")]
    R2 --> S2[("LSM storage")]
    R3 --> S3[("LSM storage")]
    G["Gossip membership"] -.-> CO
    G -.-> R1
```

Walk a write with N = 3, W = 2: the client hashes `cart:42`, finds its preference list (A, B, C) and sends the put to A, which acts as coordinator. A stamps a version, writes locally and forwards to B and C in parallel. As soon as two replicas (including itself) acknowledge, A returns success; C's write completes in the background. A quorum read with R = 2 asks two replicas, returns the newest version and, if they differ, writes the newest back to the stale one (**read repair**). Because R + W > N, every read quorum overlaps every write quorum in at least one node, so in the absence of failures a quorum read sees the latest acknowledged write.

## Deep dives

### 1. Partitioning that survives growth (elasticity)

**Bad: `hash(key) mod N`.** Going from 30 to 31 nodes remaps about 97% of keys, a near-total reshuffle of 30 TB.

**Good: consistent hashing.** Nodes and keys share one ring; a key belongs to the next node clockwise. Adding a node takes over only the range between it and its predecessor: about 1/N of the data. But with one token per node, ranges are uneven and a new node takes load from a single neighbour.

**Great: virtual nodes (or fixed partitions).** With 256 tokens per node, a joining node takes small slices from every existing node, ranges average out, and heterogeneous hardware gets proportionally more tokens. An alternative used by several systems is a fixed number of partitions (say 4,096) assigned to nodes by a placement service; rebalancing then moves whole partitions, which is easier to reason about and to throttle.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    K["key cart:42"] -->|"murmur3"| H["ring position 0x7A..."]
    H --> T1["next token: vnode of A (zone 1)"]
    T1 --> T2["next distinct node: B (zone 2)"]
    T2 --> T3["next distinct node: C (zone 3)"]
    T3 --> PL["preference list A, B, C"]
```

The coordinator walks the ring clockwise from the key's position, skipping tokens owned by nodes or zones it has already chosen, until it has N replicas in N zones.

### 2. Quorums and staying writable (availability vs consistency)

N, R and W are knobs:

| Setting | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| N=3, W=1, R=1 | Fastest; reads may be stale; one ack before data is on one disk |
| N=3, W=2, R=2 | Read and write quorums overlap; tolerates one replica down |
| N=3, W=3, R=1 | Fast reads, but any replica down blocks writes |

**Bad: strict quorum on fixed replicas.** If two of A, B, C are unreachable, writes fail, violating "always writable".

**Great: sloppy quorum with hinted handoff.** If C is down, the coordinator writes to the next healthy node D on the ring with a **hint** ("this belongs to C"). W is satisfied by healthy nodes; when gossip reports C back, D replays the hint and deletes it. The cost: a sloppy quorum can be satisfied by nodes outside the preference list, so R + W > N no longer guarantees overlap during failures. Say this explicitly; it is the price of "always writable".

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant CL as Client
    participant A as Coordinator A
    participant B as Replica B
    participant C as Replica C (down)
    participant D as Fallback D
    CL->>A: put(cart:42, v2), W=2
    A->>A: write locally
    A->>B: replicate
    A-xC: replicate (timeout)
    A->>D: replicate with hint for C
    B-->>A: ack
    A-->>CL: success (A and B acked)
    D-->>A: ack (hint stored)
    Note over D,C: when C recovers, D replays the hint to C
```

The client gets success after two acks. The fallback node holds C's copy so the system still has three copies, and hands it back once C is healthy.

### 3. Resolving conflicting versions (consistency semantics)

With sloppy quorums and partitions, two clients can write the same key on different replicas concurrently.

**Bad: wall-clock last-write-wins without discussion.** Clock skew of even a few milliseconds silently discards a newer write, and for a shopping cart a concurrent "add item" is lost.

**Good: last-write-wins with hybrid logical clocks.** Every version carries a timestamp; replicas keep the larger. Simple, bounded metadata, and right when values are whole-object replacements where losing a concurrent write is acceptable (user profile, session blob). Cassandra applies LWW per column.

**Great when merges matter: vector clocks (or dotted version vectors).** Each version carries a small map of `{node: counter}`. If one clock dominates the other, the newer one wins; if neither dominates, the writes were concurrent and the store keeps both as **siblings**, returning them on the next read for the application to merge (union of cart items) and write back with the merged context. For common data types, CRDTs (counters, sets, maps) merge automatically. The trade-off is metadata size and pushing merge logic to clients.

Deletes write a **tombstone** rather than removing data, so an old replica cannot resurrect the key during anti-entropy. Tombstones are purged after a grace period longer than the maximum time a replica can be offline before being rebuilt.

### 4. Detecting failures and repairing divergence (durability)

**Failure detection via gossip.** Each node, every second, exchanges membership and heartbeat counters with a few random peers. Information spreads in O(log N) rounds with no central coordinator. Use a phi-accrual or timeout-based detector to mark a node *suspected*, and distinguish temporary failure (hinted handoff) from permanent removal (an operator or automation reassigns its ranges).

Three repair mechanisms work at different time scales:

- **Read repair:** fixes the keys that are actually read, during the read.
- **Hinted handoff:** fixes writes missed during short outages.
- **Anti-entropy with Merkle trees:** fixes everything else, such as lost hints and cold keys.

Comparing 1 TB of keys between two replicas by streaming them is too expensive. Instead each replica builds a **Merkle tree** per token range: leaves are hashes of key buckets, parents are hashes of children. Two replicas exchange root hashes; if equal, the range is identical. If not, they descend only into differing children, so the data exchanged is proportional to the differences, not the range size.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    RA["Replica A root hash"] --> CMP{"roots equal?"}
    RB["Replica B root hash"] --> CMP
    CMP -->|"yes"| DONE["range in sync"]
    CMP -->|"no"| L["compare child hashes"]
    L --> DIFF["descend only into mismatched children"]
    DIFF --> LEAF["mismatched leaf buckets"]
    LEAF --> SYNC["stream just those keys, newest version wins"]
```

Repair runs continuously in the background, throttled so it does not compete with foreground traffic.

### 5. Storage engine for write-heavy load (latency and throughput)

**Bad: update B-tree pages in place with fsync per write.** At 77k replica-ops/s per node, random writes and page splits saturate the disk.

**Great: log-structured merge tree.** Each write is appended to a **write-ahead log** (sequential, group-committed fsync for durability) and inserted into an in-memory sorted **memtable**. When the memtable reaches ~64 MB it is flushed as an immutable sorted **SSTable**. Reads check the memtable, then SSTables from newest to oldest, skipping files whose **Bloom filter** says the key is absent (about 1% false positives at 10 bits per key). Background **compaction** merges SSTables, drops overwritten versions and expired tombstones, and keeps read amplification bounded. Choose leveled compaction for read-heavy tables (less space and read amplification) or size-tiered for write-heavy ones (less write amplification). RocksDB is a common embedded choice.

The trade-off is amplification: LSM trees trade higher write amplification from compaction and occasional read amplification for sequential, fast writes. Compaction storms can hurt p99, so throttle compaction I/O and monitor pending compaction bytes.

**Beyond one region.** Run an independent ring per region and replicate asynchronously between regions, with conflict resolution from deep dive 3. Clients choose `local_quorum` to keep latency in-region.

## What interviewers look for

- **Mid-level:** consistent hashing instead of mod-N, replication across zones, an explanation of R + W > N, and a basic failure story.
- **Senior:** virtual nodes and rebalancing cost, sloppy quorum and hinted handoff with the honest consistency caveat, a conflict-resolution choice justified by the data type, tombstones, and a storage engine choice backed by the per-node throughput estimate.
- **Staff:** ties the knobs to product SLAs per table, explains operational risks (compaction storms, repair bandwidth, gossip convergence, hot partitions), compares fixed-partition placement with vnodes, and maps out multi-region semantics and how clients should reason about anomalies.

## Common mistakes

- Using `hash mod N` and then hand-waving rebalancing.
- Claiming R + W > N gives strong consistency while also using sloppy quorums.
- Picking last-write-wins by wall clock without noticing it silently drops concurrent updates.
- Deleting keys physically, so anti-entropy resurrects them.
- Ignoring zone placement: three replicas in one zone survive a disk failure but not a zone outage.
- Describing Merkle trees without explaining why they beat streaming every key.

## Self-review checklist

- [ ] Adding a node moves roughly 1/N of the data, and you can show why.
- [ ] Replicas are placed in distinct failure domains.
- [ ] R, W and N are chosen per use case, with the failure each tolerates.
- [ ] You stated where the design is not linearizable.
- [ ] Concurrent writes have a defined resolution, and deletes use tombstones with a grace period.
- [ ] Short outages, missed reads and long-term divergence each have a repair mechanism.
- [ ] The storage engine choice follows from the write rate per node.

## Further reading

- [Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (SOSP 2007)](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)
- [Apache Cassandra documentation: architecture](https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/latest/cassandra/architecture/index.html)
- [RocksDB wiki](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki)
keyTakeaways: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes moves about 1/N of the data when a node joins; mod-N reshuffles nearly everything.
R + W > N makes read and write quorums overlap, but sloppy quorums trade that guarantee for staying writable during failures.
Last-write-wins is simple but drops concurrent updates; vector clocks or CRDTs preserve them at the cost of metadata and merge logic.
Read repair, hinted handoff and Merkle-tree anti-entropy fix divergence at different time scales; deletes need tombstones.
A high per-node write rate is the reason to choose an LSM tree with a WAL, memtable, SSTables, Bloom filters and compaction.
